title: Mix-method toolbox for monitoring greenhouse gas production and microbiome responses
author: Lourenço, Suleiman, et al.
materials: The methods selected to determine the variables can vary based on the resources and equipment available. In the study, soil moisture was determined gravimetrically by drying the soil at 105 °C for 24 h, and all results were expressed per gram of dry soil. The water-filled pore space (WFPS) was calculated considering soil moisture, soil bulk density and porosity determined at the beginning of the experiment [28]. The mineral N was extracted with 1 M KCl in 1:10 soil-to-solution ratio and the concentrations of NH4+ [29] and NO3− [30] in the filtered extract were determined colorimetrically by flow injection analysis (FIAlab-2500 System). The air and soil temperatures were measured using a digital soil thermometer. Climatic data were obtained from a meteorological station located approximately 500 m from the experimented area.

A diverse range of kits for isolating DNA is available, and in this study, the MoBio PowerSoil DNA Isolation Kit (MoBio, Solana Beach, CA, USA) was employed. Total DNA was extracted from 0.25 g of each soil sample following the manufacturer's instructions. All DNA samples were stored at −20 °C until they were used in downstream analyses. Three replicates of each vinasse batch were also used for DNA extraction. To extract the DNA from an amendment such as vinasse, two 50-mL aliquots of each vinasse replicate were centrifuged at 10,621 g for 10 min using a benchtop centrifuge (Sigma 2–16P) to separate the cells from the liquid. The resulting pellets were then combined for further analysis. This can applied also to manure, slurry, compost, etc. Total DNA was extracted from the pellets using the MoBio PowerSoil DNA Isolation Kit (MoBio, Solana Beach, CA, USA) following the manufacturer's instructions. The concentration and quality of both soil and vinasse DNA samples were assessed spectrophotometrically (NanoDrop 1000, Thermo Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA), fluorometrically (Qubit 2.0 Fluorometer, Life Technologies, Carlsbad, CA, USA), and via agarose gel electrophoresis (Tris-acetate-EDTA (TAE) buffer, 1% w/v).

In the study, gene abundance was assessed in gene copies per gram of dry soil. Spearman correlation analysis (Systat Software, 2014) was employed to calculate the correlations between microbial gene abundance and N2O flux. Furthermore, to assess the relative impacts of functional genes, treatments, and climatic factors on N2O emissions, a general linear model was applied for both seasons. The general linear model incorporated the lasso penalty and was computed using cyclical coordinate descent along a regularization path, following the approach outlined by Friedman et al. [50]. Log10 transformation was applied to N2O and gene abundance data (including N2O, 16S rRNA, and 18S rRNA, archaeal and bacterial amoA, fungal and bacterial nirK, bacterial nirS, and nosZ), as well as standardized soil factor variables. The lasso penalty, a regression method performing variable selection and shrinkage, was employed [51]. Cross-validation criteria with the “one standard error” rule were adopted, checking the lambda value that minimized the mean square error and selecting the largest value of lambda within one standard error of the minimum, to determine the most appropriate model [27]. This criterion enabled the selection of a model minimizing both the selected variables and square error. Treatments were incorporated as dummy variables, and the analysis was conducted using the “GLMNET” package in the R environment [50].

The 16S ribosomal RNA (rRNA) gene is a key component of the bacterial genome, and it is important for the identification and classification of bacterial species. It contains both conserved regions, which are similar across all bacteria, and variable regions, which exhibit variations that are unique to different bacterial taxa. These variable regions are crucial for distinguishing between bacterial species or genera. Different variable regions of the 16S rRNA gene can be targeted for sequencing, and the choice of region depends on the research goals and the level of taxonomic resolution required. In the study, the variable V4 region of bacterial 16S rRNA gene was utilized as targets for the analyses of Illumina 16S rRNA gene sequencing using the universal bacterial primers 515F (5′-GTGCCAGC MGCCGCGGTAA-3′) and 806R (5′- GGACTACHVGGGTWTCTAAT-3′) resulting in amplicons of ∼300–350 bp [52,53]. The primers already contain barcodes and sequencing adapters. The reactions were made in triplicate, they were performed in a total volume 25 µl containing 18.3 µl of H2O, 2.5 µl of 10X PCR-buffer + magnesium, 2.5 µl of dNTPs (2 mM), 0.20 µl of fast startExp-Polymerase (5 U µL−1), 0.25 µl of each primer (10 pmol µl−1) (forward and reverse) and 1 µl of DNA template in a thermocycler (Bio-Rad, CA, USA) with the following conditions: initial denaturation for 5 min at 95 °C, followed by 35 cycles of 30 s at 95 °C, 30 s at 53 °C and 60 s at 72 °C and a final extension for 10 min at 72 °C. Each sample was purified with Agencourt AMPure XP beads (Beckman Colter, Berea, CA, USA), and the library quality was assessed on a Qubit 2.0 Fluorometer (Thermo Scientific) and an Agilent Fragment Analyzer system. The samples were pooled based on the concentration of 20 ng ul-1 of DNA for each sample. Dual-index and Illumina sequencing adapters were attached to the V4 amplicons. The mixture of PCR products was subjected to paired-end sequencing using a MiSeq Reagent Kit v3 on the Illumina MiSeq Sequencing platform on the Illumina MiSeq System at BGI Genomics, China.

The Internal Transcribed Spacer (ITS) region is a genetic marker commonly used in the study of fungal diversity and taxonomy. Similar to the 16S rRNA gene for bacteria, the ITS region is used to characterize and identify different fungal species based on genetic variations. The ITS region comprises two distinct subregions: ITS1 and ITS2, separated by the 5.8S rRNA gene. These regions are found within the ribosomal RNA gene cluster in the fungal genome. The fungal ribosomal internal transcribed spacers (region ITS2) region was utilized as targets for the analyses of Illumina ITS gene sequencing. The ITS2 primers ITS9F [57] and ITS4R [58] primers (5′GAACGCAGCRAAIIGYGA-3′ and 5′-TCCTCCGCTTATTGATATGC-3′) with barcodes were used for PCRs amplifications. The reaction was conducted in 25 µl containing 15.6 µl of H2O, 2.5 µl of 10X PCR-buffer + magnesium, 2.5 µl of dNTPs (2 mM), 0.15 µl of fast startExp-Polymerase (5 U/µL), 1 µl of MgCl2 (25 mM), 1.25 µl of BSA, 0.5 µl of each primer (forward and reverse) and 1 µl of DNA template in a thermocycler (Bio-Rad, CA, USA) with the following conditions: initial denaturation for 5 min at 95 °C, followed by 40 cycles of 45 s at 95 °C, 60 s at 54 °C and 90 s at 72 °C and a final extension for 10 min at 72 °C. Each sample was purified with Agencourt AMPure XP beads (Beckman Colter, Berea, CA, USA), and the library quality was assessed on a Qubit 2.0 Fluorometer (Thermo Scientific) and an Agilent Fragment Analyzer system. The samples were pooled based on the concentration of 20 ng/ul of DNA for each sample. Finally, the mixture of PCR products was subjected to paired-end sequencing using a MiSeq Reagent Kit v3 on the Illumina MiSeq Sequencing platform at BGI Genomics, China.

steps.title: Calculate and apply vinasse (V)
steps.instruction: Determine the vinasse (V) application rate as 100 m³ ha⁻¹ (10 000 m² ha⁻¹) based on the average K concentration (2 g K₂O L⁻¹) and sugarcane K uptake (185 kg K₂O ha⁻¹). Spray the calculated volume over the entire experimental plot using a motor‑driven pump with a flow regulator (Figure S3).

steps.title: Calculate and apply concentrated vinasse (CV)
steps.instruction: Apply concentrated vinasse (CV) in bands 10–20 cm from the sugarcane row at a rate of 17.2 m³ ha⁻¹ (≈5.8 × less than V) using a calibrated plastic watering can; the CV‑treated area represents ~16–20 % of the total plot (≈1 600–2 000 m² ha⁻¹).

steps.title: Apply inorganic N, P, K fertilizers
steps.instruction: Surface‑apply inorganic fertilizers in a 0.25 m‑wide band (≈16 % of total area). Use 100 kg N ha⁻¹ (as ammonium nitrate), 45 kg P₂O₅ ha⁻¹ (as superphosphate), and KCl to match the K added by vinasse: 290 kg K₂O ha⁻¹ in experiment R1, 345 kg K₂O ha⁻¹ in D1, and 320 kg K₂O ha⁻¹ in R2.

steps.title: Collect soil samples in parallel with gas sampling
steps.instruction: At each gas‑sampling event, collect six soil cores per block from the 0–10 cm layer (topsoil) for moisture, pH, WFPS, NO₃⁻‑N, NH₄⁺‑N analyses; also record air and soil temperatures with a digital soil thermometer. Schedule intensive sampling immediately after fertilizer application and after rain events, especially during the first period when N₂O peaks are expected.

steps.title: Store soil samples for chemical and molecular work
steps.instruction: Place 30 g of each soil sample in a freezer at –20 °C for chemical analyses; keep an additional aliquot at –80 °C for DNA/RNA extraction. Transport fresh samples for mineral‑N analysis in insulated containers with ice to keep them cold until laboratory processing.

steps.title: Extract DNA from soil samples
steps.instruction: Use the MoBio PowerSoil DNA Isolation Kit (MoBio, Solana Beach, CA, USA) to extract total DNA from 0.25 g of each frozen soil sample following the manufacturer’s protocol. Store the extracted DNA at –20 °C until downstream applications.

steps.title: Extract DNA from vinasse samples
steps.instruction: For each vinasse batch, take two 50‑mL aliquots, centrifuge at 10 621 g for 10 min (Sigma 2‑16P). Combine the resulting pellets, then extract DNA from the combined pellet with the MoBio PowerSoil kit as for soil. Perform the same extraction for three vinasse replicates.

steps.title: Assess DNA quantity and quality
steps.instruction: Measure DNA concentration and purity with a NanoDrop 1000 (Thermo Scientific), a Qubit 2.0 Fluorometer (Life Technologies), and verify integrity by 1 % agarose gel electrophoresis in TAE buffer.

steps.title: Amplify bacterial 16S V4 region
steps.instruction: Set up triplicate PCRs (25 µL total) containing 18.3 µL H₂O, 2.5 µL 10× PCR buffer + Mg²⁺, 2.5 µL 2 mM dNTPs, 0.20 µL FastStart‑Exp‑Polymerase (5 U µL⁻¹), 0.25 µL each primer (10 pmol µL⁻¹) – forward 515F (5′‑GTGCCAGCMGCCGCGGTAA‑3′) and reverse 806R (5′‑GGACTACHVGGGTWTCTAAT‑3′) – and 1 µL DNA template. Thermocycle: 95 °C 5 min; 35 cycles of 95 °C 30 s, 53 °C 30 s, 72 °C 60 s; final extension 72 °C 10 min.

steps.title: Purify 16S PCR products and prepare library
steps.instruction: Clean each PCR replicate with Agencourt AMPure XP beads (Beckman Coulter). Quantify purified amplicons on a Qubit 2.0 and assess fragment size on an Agilent Fragment Analyzer. Normalize all samples to 20 ng µL⁻¹, pool them, and ligate Illumina dual‑index adapters to the V4 amplicons.

steps.title: Sequence bacterial amplicons on Illumina MiSeq
steps.instruction: Load the pooled library onto an Illumina MiSeq using a MiSeq Reagent Kit v3 (paired‑end) at BGI Genomics, China, following the manufacturer’s run parameters.

steps.title: Amplify fungal ITS2 region
steps.instruction: Prepare 25 µL PCRs with 15.6 µL H₂O, 2.5 µL 10× PCR buffer + Mg²⁺, 2.5 µL 2 mM dNTPs, 0.15 µL FastStart‑Exp‑Polymerase (5 U µL⁻¹), 1 µL 25 mM MgCl₂, 1.25 µL BSA, 0.5 µL each primer (10 pmol µL⁻¹) – forward ITS9F (5′‑GAACGCAGCRAAIIGYGA‑3′) and reverse ITS4R (5′‑TCCTCCGCTTATTGATATGC‑3′) – and 1 µL DNA template. Thermocycle: 95 °C 5 min; 40 cycles of 95 °C 45 s, 54 °C 60 s, 72 °C 90 s; final extension 72 °C 10 min.

steps.title: Purify fungal PCR products and prepare library
steps.instruction: Purify the ITS amplicons with Agencourt AMPure XP beads, quantify with Qubit 2.0, check size on an Agilent Fragment Analyzer, normalize to 20 ng µL⁻¹, pool, and attach Illumina dual‑index adapters.

steps.title: Sequence fungal amplicons on Illumina MiSeq
steps.instruction: Run the pooled ITS library on an Illumina MiSeq using a MiSeq Reagent Kit v3 (paired‑end) at BGI Genomics, China.

steps.title: Process 16S sequencing data
steps.instruction: Demultiplex reads by barcode, filter for Phred ≥ 25, expected errors ≤ 0.5, and length ≥ 200 bp. Merge paired ends with PANDAseq (minimum overlap = 50 bp). Cluster sequences into OTUs at 97 % similarity using UPARSE, discard singletons, remove chimeras with UCHIME (de‑novo mode), and assign taxonomy via BLAST against Greengenes 13.5 (confidence ≥ 80 %).

steps.title: Process ITS sequencing data
steps.instruction: Demultiplex reads, filter quality and length, trim adapters, and remove PhiX using BBDuk2 (BBMap suite). Overlap paired ends with VSEARCH. Cluster OTUs at 97 % similarity using usearch_global, discard singletons, remove chimeras with UCHIME (de‑novo), and assign taxonomy with the RDP Classifier against the UNITE 7.2 database (confidence ≥ 80 %).

steps.title: Calculate bacterial and fungal alpha diversity
steps.instruction: Rarefy OTU tables, then compute observed richness, Chao1, Simpson, and Shannon indices in QIIME 1.9 for each sample.

steps.title: Assess beta diversity and community differences
steps.instruction: Perform PERMDISP2 in PRIMER v7 to test dispersion, run PERMANOVA with the vegan R package (10 000 permutations) to test treatment effects, generate PCoA plots for 16S data in QIIME 1.9, and conduct DAPC for ITS data using the adegenet R package.

steps.title: Run multivariate regression tree (MRT) analysis
steps.instruction: Log‑transform OTU abundances, then apply the mvpart function to build MRTs based on Bray–Curtis distances; use 500 cross‑validations to prune the tree and plot the PCoA of the MRT with rpart.pca.

steps.title: Identify indicator taxa with LEfSe
steps.instruction: Upload the normalized relative abundance matrix to Microbiome Analyst, run LEfSe using the Kruskal–Wallis test (α ≤ 0.05) followed by LDA to estimate effect size of discriminative families.

steps.title: Conduct co‑inertia and redundancy analyses
steps.instruction: Compute co‑inertia analysis of bacterial and fungal OTU tables with the ade4 R package; perform redundancy analysis (RDA) of microbial communities versus physicochemical variables and GHG fluxes using CANOCO 5 (Hellinger‑transformed OTU table).

steps.title: Statistical analysis of GHG emission data
steps.instruction: Test cumulative emissions for normality; if needed, apply Box‑Cox transformation (Statistica v10 or any software). Use total cumulative emissions from chambers (mg N₂O‑N m⁻²) for analysis. Conduct orthogonal contrasts with SISVAR for incomplete factorial designs. Calculate N₂O‑N emission factor (EF %) using: EF = [(N₂O_treat – N₂O_control) / N_applied(fert + Vinasse)] × 100. For field‑scale EF, apply equations: EF_V = {[(N₂O_treat × 1600)+(N₂O_Vinasse × 8400)] – (N₂O_control × 10 000)} / N_applied × 100; EF_NorCV = {[(N₂O_treat × 2000)+(N₂O_control × 8000)] – (N₂O_control × 10 000)} / N_applied × 100. Multiply chamber emissions by 1.6 for treatments applied only in the 0.25 m band, and by 1.6 + 8.4 for V treatments (band + inter‑row).
